elements.element: The Agreement imposes no non-compete restriction on the Company (Customer).
elements.evidence: Section 6.1 affirmatively states that the Company has no restriction under the Agreement on the products it may offer or the projects or websites in which it may participate.

elements.element: The Agreement imposes no field-of-use restriction on the Company (Customer).
elements.evidence: Section 6.1 removes HDI's exclusive right concerning use of the Deerskin brand and confirms that the Company is unrestricted as to products, projects, and websites.

elements.element: Any restriction on the Company is limited to a specifically named competing product.
elements.evidence: No restriction on the Company remains, so the condition requiring a restriction to be limited to a named competing product is demonstrably absent.

elements.element: Any restriction applies only during the term of the Agreement.
elements.evidence: No restriction on the Company remains during or after the term, so there is no restriction extending beyond the term.

elements.element: Any restriction is capped at 12 months.
elements.evidence: No restriction on the Company remains, so there is no restricted period exceeding 12 months.

elements.element: Any restriction carves out the Company's internal development.
elements.evidence: Because Section 6.1 imposes no restriction on the Company's products, projects, or websites, internal development is unrestricted without needing an express carve-out.

elements.element: Any restriction carves out acquisitions by the Company.
elements.evidence: Because Section 6.1 imposes no restriction on the Company, acquisitions are not subject to a non-compete or field-of-use restriction and no express carve-out is necessary.

result.reason: The operative redline fully reaches the preferred position by eliminating both the Company's non-compete and HDI's field-of-use exclusivity. The fallback limitations are also satisfied because their triggering condition—the existence of a restriction—is demonstrably absent. The changes are confined to the restrictive and exclusivity language, while the term and unrelated provisions remain effective. Drafting is clear overall, although “exclusive right to use of” is grammatically awkward and Section 6.2 is now largely redundant.
